claim: Diffusion tensor imaging was applied in healthy participants alongside an odd-one-out paradigm sensitive to PrC and HC lesions in animals and humans.
source: Diffusion tensor imaging was applied in healthy participants alongside an odd-one-out paradigm sensitive to PrC and HC lesions in animals and humans.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology used in the study, including DTI and the oddity paradigm, and references its sensitivity to lesions based on prior research.

claim: Microstructure of inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF, connecting occipital and ventro-anterior temporal lobe, including PrC) correlated with accuracy on odd-one-out judgements involving faces.
source: Microstructure of inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF, connecting occipital and ventro-anterior temporal lobe, including PrC) and fornix (the main HC input/output pathway) correlated with accuracy on odd-one-out judgements involving faces and scenes, respectively.
evidence: The abstract states the main finding that ILF microstructure correlates with face oddity performance, supported by experimental data.

claim: Fornix (the main HC input/output pathway) correlated with accuracy on odd-one-out judgements involving scenes.
source: Microstructure of inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF, connecting occipital and ventro-anterior temporal lobe, including PrC) and fornix (the main HC input/output pathway) correlated with accuracy on odd-one-out judgements involving faces and scenes, respectively.
evidence: The abstract states the main finding that fornix microstructure correlates with scene oddity performance, supported by experimental data.

claim: Blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) response in PrC, elicited during oddity judgements, was correlated with face oddity performance.
source: Similarly, blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) response in PrC and HC, elicited during oddity judgements, was correlated with face and scene oddity performance, respectively.
evidence: The abstract reports the correlation between PrC BOLD response and face oddity performance based on fMRI data.

claim: Blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) response in HC, elicited during oddity judgements, was correlated with scene oddity performance.
source: Similarly, blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) response in PrC and HC, elicited during oddity judgements, was correlated with face and scene oddity performance, respectively.
evidence: The abstract reports the correlation between HC BOLD response and scene oddity performance based on fMRI data.

claim: Associations were observed between ILF microstructure and category-selective BOLD response in PrC.
source: We also observed associations between ILF and fornix microstructure and category-selective BOLD response in PrC and HC, respectively.
evidence: The abstract states that ILF microstructure is associated with BOLD response in PrC, supported by experimental data.

claim: Associations were observed between fornix microstructure and category-selective BOLD response in HC.
source: We also observed associations between ILF and fornix microstructure and category-selective BOLD response in PrC and HC, respectively.
evidence: The abstract states that fornix microstructure is associated with BOLD response in HC, supported by experimental data.

claim: HC damage leads to impairments in perceiving, learning, and remembering complex scenes.
source: It has been shown, for example, that HC damage leads to impairments in perceiving, learning, and remembering complex scenes, whereas broader MTL damage, affecting both the HC and PrC, results in perceptual and mnemonic deficits for scene, but also face, stimuli (Barense et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2005b; Mundy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Broader MTL damage, affecting both the HC and PrC, results in perceptual and mnemonic deficits for scene and face stimuli.
source: It has been shown, for example, that HC damage leads to impairments in perceiving, learning, and remembering complex scenes, whereas broader MTL damage, affecting both the HC and PrC, results in perceptual and mnemonic deficits for scene, but also face, stimuli (Barense et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2005b; Mundy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Patients with MTL damage are able to perform perceptual discriminations on the basis of simple visual features (e.g., size and colour).
source: Critically, however, these same patients are able to perform perceptual discriminations on the basis of simple visual features (e.g., size and colour) and can learn to discriminate between complex dot patterns (Mundy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Patients with MTL damage can learn to discriminate between complex dot patterns.
source: Critically, however, these same patients are able to perform perceptual discriminations on the basis of simple visual features (e.g., size and colour) and can learn to discriminate between complex dot patterns (Mundy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Functional MRI studies show differential recruitment of the HC and PrC for scene and face discriminations, respectively.
source: These findings have been complemented by functional MRI (fMRI) studies showing (a) differential recruitment of the HC and PrC for scene and face discriminations, respectively, including on tasks analogous to those affected in lesion patients (Barense et al., 2010), and (b) modulations of blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) response by visual feature overlap in both MTL (high > low) and occipito-temporal (low > high) regions (Mundy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: BOLD response is modulated by visual feature overlap in both MTL (high > low) and occipito-temporal (low > high) regions.
source: These findings have been complemented by functional MRI (fMRI) studies showing (a) differential recruitment of the HC and PrC for scene and face discriminations, respectively, including on tasks analogous to those affected in lesion patients (Barense et al., 2010), and (b) modulations of blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) response by visual feature overlap in both MTL (high > low) and occipito-temporal (low > high) regions (Mundy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an fMRI study.

claim: Hierarchical, representational theories propose that perceptual difficulties in patients with MTL involvement reflect damage to conjunctive scene and face/object representations stored within the HC and PrC, respectively.
source: Emerging hierarchical, representational theories provide a framework for such investigations (Graham et al., 2010; Saksida and Bussey, 2010); they propose that perceptual difficulties in patients with MTL involvement reflect damage to conjunctive scene and face/object representations stored within the HC and PrC, respectively (Murray et al., 2007; Graham et al., 2010; Saksida and Bussey, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Any task, whether perceptual or mnemonic, that places demand on conjunctive representations is predicted to lead to impairment in patients with MTL damage.
source: Any task, whether perceptual or mnemonic, that places demand on these conjunctive representations, such as discriminating between exemplars with many overlapping features (Saksida and Bussey, 2010), is predicted to lead to impairment.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical predictions from representational accounts.

claim: Processing of visual exemplars with minimal overlap can be supported by posterior visual cortical regions.
source: By contrast, processing of visual exemplars with minimal overlap can be supported by posterior visual cortical regions (Barense et al., 2010; Mundy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Macaque monkeys with lesions to the PrC are impaired on oddity tasks when presented with face and object arrays.
source: For example, macaque monkeys with lesions to the PrC are impaired on oddity tasks when presented with face and object arrays (Buckley et al., 2001); this pattern is also seen in amnesic patients when damage to the MTL includes PrC (Lee et al., 2005a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to animal lesion studies.

claim: Amnesic patients with damage to the MTL that includes PrC are impaired on oddity tasks when presented with face and object arrays.
source: For example, macaque monkeys with lesions to the PrC are impaired on oddity tasks when presented with face and object arrays (Buckley et al., 2001); this pattern is also seen in amnesic patients when damage to the MTL includes PrC (Lee et al., 2005a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to human lesion studies.

claim: Patients with selective damage to the HC perform as well as controls on face and object oddity judgements.
source: Conversely, patients with selective damage to the HC perform as well as controls on face and object oddity judgements, but show impairments for scene oddity decisions (Lee et al., 2005a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to human lesion studies.

claim: Patients with selective damage to the HC show impairments for scene oddity decisions.
source: Conversely, patients with selective damage to the HC perform as well as controls on face and object oddity judgements, but show impairments for scene oddity decisions (Lee et al., 2005a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to human lesion studies.

claim: The fornix is a major input and output pathway of the HC.
source: The fornix—a major input and output pathway of the HC—has long been considered to form part of an extended hippocampal system, both in terms of its role in episodic memory (Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2011), but also in spatial processing (Bird and Burgess, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The fornix has long been considered to form part of an extended hippocampal system in terms of its role in episodic memory.
source: The fornix—a major input and output pathway of the HC—has long been considered to form part of an extended hippocampal system, both in terms of its role in episodic memory (Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2011), but also in spatial processing (Bird and Burgess, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The fornix has long been considered to form part of an extended hippocampal system in terms of its role in spatial processing.
source: The fornix—a major input and output pathway of the HC—has long been considered to form part of an extended hippocampal system, both in terms of its role in episodic memory (Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2011), but also in spatial processing (Bird and Burgess, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Fornix transection in non-human primates impairs learning of object-in-place associations.
source: For example, the impact of fornix transection in non-human primates suggests that exchange of information between HC and diencephalic regions is necessary for learning both object-in-place associations and conjunctions of spatial features (Gaffan, 1994; Buckley et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to animal lesion studies.

claim: Fornix transection in non-human primates impairs learning of conjunctions of spatial features.
source: For example, the impact of fornix transection in non-human primates suggests that exchange of information between HC and diencephalic regions is necessary for learning both object-in-place associations and conjunctions of spatial features (Gaffan, 1994; Buckley et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to animal lesion studies.

claim: Fornix damage in humans impairs episodic memory, as assessed by standardised neuropsychological tasks.
source: Fornix damage in humans also impairs episodic memory, as assessed by standardised neuropsychological tasks (Tsivilis et al., 2008), and fornix microstructure has been shown to correlate with scene recollection (Rudebeck et al., 2009), suggesting a potential convergence between findings in human and non-human primates.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to human lesion studies.

claim: Fornix microstructure has been shown to correlate with scene recollection.
source: Fornix damage in humans also impairs episodic memory, as assessed by standardised neuropsychological tasks (Tsivilis et al., 2008), and fornix microstructure has been shown to correlate with scene recollection (Rudebeck et al., 2009), suggesting a potential convergence between findings in human and non-human primates.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The ILF serves as the primary input pathway to the antero-medial temporal lobe, including PrC.
source: A second relevant white matter (WM) pathway is the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF). This tract serves as the primary input pathway to the antero-medial temporal lobe, including PrC (Catani et al., 2003), and is comprised mainly of long association fibres connecting extrastriate visual areas with regions in ventral anterior temporal (vATL) cortex (Latini, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The ILF is comprised mainly of long association fibres connecting extrastriate visual areas with regions in ventral anterior temporal (vATL) cortex.
source: A second relevant white matter (WM) pathway is the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF). This tract serves as the primary input pathway to the antero-medial temporal lobe, including PrC (Catani et al., 2003), and is comprised mainly of long association fibres connecting extrastriate visual areas with regions in ventral anterior temporal (vATL) cortex (Latini, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to anatomical studies.

claim: Individuals with congenital prosopagnosia have altered WM microstructure relative to matched controls in ILF.
source: Indeed, there is evidence suggesting that ILF microstructure is related to performance in tasks involving face stimuli; for example, individuals with congenital prosopagnosia (CP, a syndrome characterised by impairments in identifying faces) have altered WM microstructure and macrostructure (i.e., volume) relative to matched controls in ILF (Thomas et al., 2009; Gomez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals with congenital prosopagnosia have altered WM macrostructure (i.e., volume) relative to matched controls in ILF.
source: Indeed, there is evidence suggesting that ILF microstructure is related to performance in tasks involving face stimuli; for example, individuals with congenital prosopagnosia (CP, a syndrome characterised by impairments in identifying faces) have altered WM microstructure and macrostructure (i.e., volume) relative to matched controls in ILF (Thomas et al., 2009; Gomez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

source: Based on this, we predicted that individual success on scene oddity would correlate negatively with fornix MD and positively with fornix FA.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: Measures obtained from fornix and ILF would not be associated with performance on an equally difficult size oddity control condition.
source: Furthermore, we hypothesised that measures obtained from these pathways would not be associated with performance on an equally difficult size oddity control condition, which is unaffected following damage to MTL (Buckley et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis made by the authors based on prior lesion studies.

claim: The relationship between regional activity in HC and PrC/FFA and scene and face oddity accuracy, respectively, may be partially mediated by inter-individual variation in fornix and ILF WM microstructure, respectively.
source: Finally, we used a mediation analysis (Hayes, 2013) to examine the three-way relationship between regional functional activity, WM microstructure, and oddity performance. If broader MTL neural circuits support complex visual discrimination, then the relationship between regional activity in HC and PrC/FFA and scene and face oddity accuracy, respectively, may be partially mediated by inter-individual variation in fornix and ILF WM microstructure, respectively.
evidence: This is a hypothesis made by the authors based on theoretical reasoning.

evidence: The claim is based on whole-brain TBSS analysis.

claim: The peak for the largest FA cluster was located in the right callosal body (16, 12, 29; p = 0.00) and incorporated several prominent WM structures bilaterally, including ILF, SLF, and forceps major.
source: The peak for the largest cluster was located in the right callosal body (16, 12, 29; p = 0.00) and incorporated several prominent WM structures bilaterally, including ILF, SLF, and forceps major (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on whole-brain TBSS analysis.

claim: A second FA cluster of 118 voxels was identified with a peak in the right anterior ILF (40, −33, −15; p = 0.05).
source: A second cluster of 118 voxels was identified with a peak in the right anterior ILF (40, −33, −15; p = 0.05).
evidence: The claim is based on whole-brain TBSS analysis.

claim: There were 250 significant voxels in ILF with the peak located in the left ILF for FA.
source: There were 250 significant voxels in ILF with the peak located in the left ILF.
evidence: The claim is based on whole-brain TBSS analysis.

claim: The statistical map reflecting a negative association between inter-subject BOLD for F > S and ILF MD revealed significant bilateral clusters in FFA (left: −28, −52, −18, Z = 2.99, 25 voxels; right: 44, −52, −18, Z = 3.07, 41 voxels).
source: As shown in Figure 3A, the statistical map reflecting a negative association between inter-subject BOLD for F > S and ILF MD revealed significant bilateral clusters in FFA (left: −28, −52, −18, Z = 2.99, 25 voxels; right: 44, −52, −18, Z = 3.07, 41 voxels).
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures, and is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a cluster of 11 voxels in left PrC (−32, −12, −34, Z = 2.81) for F > S and ILF MD, which did not quite reach the PrC cluster extent threshold (cluster >17 voxels, p = 0.05).
source: There was also a cluster of 11 voxels in left PrC (−32, −12, −34, Z = 2.81), which did not quite reach our PrC cluster extent threshold (cluster >17 voxels, p = 0.05; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures, and is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No clusters were found for F > S and ILF FA.
source: No clusters were found for F > S and ILF FA.
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures.

claim: For F > rest, significant bilateral clusters in FFA were identified associated with ILF MD (left: −28, −52, −18, Z = 2.98, 19 voxels; right: 42, −54, −18, Z = 4.21, 210 voxels).
source: As these functional associations with MD could arise from between-subject variability in the scene oddity baseline, we also conducted this analysis for F > rest; as above, we identified significant bilateral clusters in FFA associated with ILF MD, with the larger, stronger, cluster located in right hemisphere (left: −28, −52, −18, Z = 2.98, 19 voxels; right: 42, −54, −18, Z = 4.21, 210 voxels; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures, and is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For F > rest, bilateral face-sensitive clusters in the PrC were identified associated with ILF MD (left: −32, −14, −34, Z = 3.52, 19 voxels; right: 28, −16, −32, Z = 3.52, 27 voxels).
source: We also identified bilateral face-sensitive clusters in the PrC associated with ILF MD (left: −32, −14, −34, Z = 3.52, 19 voxels; right: 28, −16, −32, Z = 3.52, 27 voxels; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures, and is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There were no supra-threshold clusters in FFA or PrC for ILF FA.
source: There were no supra-threshold clusters in FFA or PrC for ILF FA.
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures.

claim: There were no significant clusters in the HC for scene contrasts (S > F or S > rest) and either measure of fornix microstructure.
source: In the HC, there were no significant clusters for our two scene contrasts (S > F or S > rest) and either measure of fornix microstructure.
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures.

claim: The S < rest contrast revealed a significant cluster in left intermediate HC (−26, −24, −16, Z = 3.1, 32 voxels) that was strongly associated with fornix FA.
source: This analysis revealed a significant cluster in left intermediate HC (−26, −24, −16, Z = 3.1, 32 voxels; Figure 3C) that was strongly associated with fornix FA.
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures, and is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The fornix MD analysis revealed a cluster in right anterior HC (20, −16, −16, Z = 2.24) at a lower voxel-wise threshold (p = 0.05).
source: The fornix MD analysis revealed a cluster in right anterior HC (20, −16, −16, Z = 2.24) albeit at a lower voxel-wise threshold (p = 0.05).
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures.

claim: The F < rest analysis revealed no voxels in HC associated with either fornix MD or FA.
source: To test whether this deactivation effect was specific to scene oddity, we conducted the same analysis for face deactivations against rest baseline (F < rest); this revealed no voxels in HC associated with either fornix MD or FA.
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures.

claim: No significant clusters were found that showed a significant positive or negative association between scene-selective BOLD (S > F, S > rest) and fornix microstructure (MD or FA) in PHG, RSC, or TOS.
source: No significant clusters were found that showed a significant positive or negative association between scene-selective BOLD (S > F, S > rest) and fornix microstructure (MD or FA) in any of the additional scene-selective ROIs.
evidence: The claim is based on ROI analysis of fMRI data correlated with DTI measures in additional scene-selective regions.

claim: A significant positive relationship was found between face-sensitive BOLD (F > rest) in FFA and face oddity accuracy (r = 0.36, p = 0.04, 95% CI [0.05, 0.65]).
source: A significant positive relationship was found between face-sensitive BOLD (F > rest) in FFA and face oddity accuracy (r = 0.36, p = 0.04, 95% CI [0.05, 0.65]; Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between BOLD response and behavioral performance, and is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A significant positive correlation was observed between BOLD for faces (F > rest) in PrC and face oddity performance (r = 0.42, p = 0.02, 95% CI [0.06, 0.69]).
source: A significant positive correlation was also observed between BOLD for faces (F > rest) in PrC and face oddity performance (r = 0.42, p = 0.02, 95% CI [0.06, 0.69]; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between BOLD response and behavioral performance, and is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neither FFA nor PrC BOLD was correlated with scene oddity performance (all ps > 0.2).
source: Neither ROI was correlated with scene oddity performance (all ps > 0.2).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between BOLD response and behavioral performance.

claim: There was a strong trend between scene-related deactivations (S < rest) and scene oddity accuracy in the HC ROI (r = 0.30, p = 0.08, 95% CI [−0.039, 0.606]).
source: There was also a strong trend evident between scene-related deactivations (S < rest) and scene oddity accuracy in the HC ROI (r = 0.30, p = 0.08, 95% CI [−0.039, 0.606]; Figure 4C); an association that was not evident for the face oddity condition (p = 0.20).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between BOLD response and behavioral performance, and is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The association between HC scene deactivations and scene oddity was not evident for the face oddity condition (p = 0.20).
source: There was also a strong trend evident between scene-related deactivations (S < rest) and scene oddity accuracy in the HC ROI (r = 0.30, p = 0.08, 95% CI [−0.039, 0.606]; Figure 4C); an association that was not evident for the face oddity condition (p = 0.20).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between BOLD response and behavioral performance.

claim: FFA BOLD activity indirectly influenced face oddity performance through its relationship with ILF MD.
source: From a mediation analysis conducted using ordinary least squares path analysis (Preacher and Hayes, 2008), FFA BOLD activity indirectly influenced face oddity performance through its relationship with ILF MD.
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis.

claim: Individuals with a higher FFA BOLD response for F > rest had significantly lower ILF MD values.
source: As seen in Figure 5A, individuals with a higher FFA BOLD response for F > rest had significantly lower ILF MD values, and participants with lower ILF MD values showed significantly better face discrimination ability.
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis, and is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Participants with lower ILF MD values showed significantly better face discrimination ability.
source: As seen in Figure 5A, individuals with a higher FFA BOLD response for F > rest had significantly lower ILF MD values, and participants with lower ILF MD values showed significantly better face discrimination ability.
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis, and is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A bootstrap 95% CI for the indirect effect of FFA BOLD on face oddity via ILF MD was entirely above zero.
source: A bootstrap 95% CI (based on 1000 bootstrapped samples) for the indirect effect was entirely above zero (see Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis, and is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was no evidence that FFA BOLD activity influenced face oddity performance independent of its relationship with ILF MD.
source: Thus, there was no evidence that FFA BOLD activity influenced face oddity performance independent of its relationship with ILF MD.
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis.

claim: The mediation effect of ILF MD on the relationship between FFA BOLD and face oddity was predominantly evident in the right hemisphere.
source: Further analyses revealed that this effect was predominantly evident in the right hemisphere (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on additional mediation analyses reported in supplementary materials.

claim: An alternative model in which FFA activity mediated the influence of ILF MD on face oddity performance revealed no evidence for an indirect effect (95% CI [−1017.19, 1361.64]).
source: An alternative model in which FFA activity mediated the influence of ILF MD on face oddity performance revealed no evidence for an indirect effect of ILF MD on face discrimination accuracy through its effect on FFA BOLD activity (95% CI [−1017.19, 1361.64]; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on alternative mediation analysis.

claim: Analysis of the PrC ROI revealed a significant direct effect of BOLD response for faces (F > rest) on face oddity success.
source: A comparable analysis for PrC revealed a significant direct effect of BOLD response for faces (F > rest) on face oddity success (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis, and is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A bootstrap 95% CI for the indirect effect of PrC BOLD on face oddity via ILF MD crossed zero and was thus non-significant (95% CI [−0.01, 0.1]).
source: A bootstrap 95% CI for the indirect effect was found to cross zero and was thus non-significant (95% CI [−0.01, 0.1]).
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis.

claim: PrC BOLD and ILF MD are independent predictors of face oddity performance.
source: This finding indicates that PrC BOLD and ILF MD are independent predictors of face oddity performance.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the mediation analysis results.

claim: The alternative mediation model in which PrC BOLD activity mediated the influence of ILF MD on face oddity revealed no evidence for an indirect effect.
source: The alternative mediation model in which PrC BOLD activity mediated the influence of ILF MD on face oddity (see Supplementary file 2) revealed no evidence for an indirect effect of ILF MD on face discrimination via its effect on PrC activity.
evidence: The claim is based on alternative mediation analysis.

claim: Analysis of the HC ROI revealed a significant direct effect of BOLD deactivation for S < rest on scene oddity.
source: Analysis of the HC ROI revealed a significant direct effect of BOLD deactivation for S < rest on scene oddity (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis, and is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The indirect effect of HC BOLD on scene oddity via fornix MD crossed zero (−0.19, −0.01), indicating that HC BOLD and fornix MD independently predicted inter-individual variations in scene oddity accuracy.
source: As the indirect effect of HC BOLD, via fornix MD, crossed zero (−0.19, −0.01), these measures independently predicted inter-individual variations in scene oddity accuracy.
evidence: The claim is based on mediation analysis.

claim: The alternative model in which HC scene deactivations mediated the influence of fornix MD on scene discrimination performance revealed no evidence for an indirect effect.
source: The alternative model in which HC scene deactivations mediated the influence of fornix MD on scene discrimination performance (see Supplementary file 2) revealed no evidence for an indirect effect of fornix MD on scene oddity via its effect on HC BOLD.
evidence: The claim is based on alternative mediation analysis.

claim: MD reflects a combined average of axial diffusion (diffusion along the principal axis) and radial diffusion (diffusion along the orthogonal direction).
source: MD (10−3 mm2 s−1) reflects a combined average of axial diffusion (diffusion along the principal axis) and radial diffusion (diffusion along the orthogonal direction), and FA reflects the extent to which diffusion within biological tissue is anisotropic, or constrained along a single axis, and can range from 0 (fully isotropic) to 1 (fully anisotropic).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about DTI metrics.

claim: FA reflects the extent to which diffusion within biological tissue is anisotropic, or constrained along a single axis, and can range from 0 (fully isotropic) to 1 (fully anisotropic).
source: MD (10−3 mm2 s−1) reflects a combined average of axial diffusion (diffusion along the principal axis) and radial diffusion (diffusion along the orthogonal direction), and FA reflects the extent to which diffusion within biological tissue is anisotropic, or constrained along a single axis, and can range from 0 (fully isotropic) to 1 (fully anisotropic).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about DTI metrics.

claim: Decreases in MD are associated with microstructural properties that are considered to support the efficient transfer of information along WM, such as increased myelination and axon density.
source: Decreases in MD (and also increases in FA) are associated, typically, with microstructural properties that are considered to support the efficient transfer of information along WM, such as increased myelination and axon density (Beaulieu, 2002; but see; Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increases in FA are associated with microstructural properties that are considered to support the efficient transfer of information along WM, such as increased myelination and axon density.
source: Decreases in MD (and also increases in FA) are associated, typically, with microstructural properties that are considered to support the efficient transfer of information along WM, such as increased myelination and axon density (Beaulieu, 2002; but see; Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Functional specialization is an emergent property of the interactions between a set of spatially distributed nodes and their functional and structural connections.
source: More specifically, it has been proposed that, 'functional specialization is not simply an intrinsic property of individual regions that compute specific representations in isolation, but rather, is an emergent property of the interactions between a set of spatially distributed nodes and their functional and structural connections' (Behrmann and Plaut, 2013, p. 211).
evidence: The claim is a direct quote from a cited theoretical paper.

claim: 30 undergraduates from Cardiff University participated in this study (2 male; aged 18–22 years; mean = 19; SD = 0.96).
source: 30 undergraduates from Cardiff University participated in this study (2 male; aged 18–22 years; mean = 19; SD = 0.96) and were paid for taking part.
evidence: The claim describes the participant sample.

claim: Cardiff University School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee approved the research project.
source: Cardiff University School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee approved the research project.
evidence: The claim describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: In the oddity task, participants were presented with three stimuli on each trial and instructed to select the odd-one-out as quickly and as accurately as possible.
source: In the oddity task, participants were presented with three stimuli on each trial (top centre; bottom left; bottom right) and instructed to select the odd-one-out as quickly and as accurately as possible.
evidence: The claim describes the task procedure.

claim: Two of the stimuli in the oddity task were the same item from different viewpoints, and the third stimulus was a different item.
source: Two of these stimuli were the same item from different viewpoints, and the third stimulus was a different item.
evidence: The claim describes the task design.

claim: Stimuli in the oddity task were presented concurrently on each trial and never repeated once shown in the task.
source: To ensure that mnemonic demand was minimised in the oddity task, stimuli were presented concurrently on each trial and never repeated, once shown, in the task (Lee et al., 2005a).
evidence: The claim describes the task design to minimize memory demands.

claim: Each trial in the oddity task was presented for 6 s with a jittered inter-trial interval of 500–4000 ms.
source: Each trial was presented for 6 s with a jittered inter-trial interval of 500–4000 ms.
evidence: The claim describes the task timing parameters.

claim: The task was administered in the scanner over three functional imaging runs.
source: The task was administered in the scanner over three functional imaging runs.
evidence: The claim describes the task administration.

claim: Within each run, trials for a given category (scene, face, size) were presented in mini-blocks of three successive trials.
source: Within each run, trials for a given category (scene, face, size) were presented in mini-blocks of three successive trials.
evidence: The claim describes the task structure.

claim: Overall, 18 trials were presented per category per run resulting in 54 trials per condition overall.
source: Overall, 18 trials were presented per category per run resulting in 54 trials per condition overall.
evidence: The claim describes the number of trials in the task.

claim: Imaging data were collected at the Cardiff University Brain Research Imaging Centre (CUBRIC) using a GE 3-T HDx MRI system with an 8-channel receive-only head coil.
source: Imaging data were collected at the Cardiff University Brain Research Imaging Centre (CUBRIC) using a GE 3-T HDx MRI system with an 8-channel receive-only head coil.
evidence: The claim describes the MRI acquisition setup.

claim: Whole-brain high angular resolution diffusion image data were acquired using a diffusion weighted single-shot spin-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) pulse sequence.
source: Whole-brain high angular resolution diffusion image data were acquired using a diffusion weighted single-shot spin-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) pulse sequence with the following parameters: TE = 87 ms; voxel dimensions = 2.4 × 2.4 × 2.4 mm3; field of view = 23 × 23 cm2; 96 × 96 acquisition matrix; 60 contiguous slices acquired along an oblique–axial plane with 2.4-mm thickness (no gap).
evidence: The claim describes the diffusion MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Acquisitions were cardiac gated using a peripheral pulse oximeter.
source: Acquisitions were cardiac gated using a peripheral pulse oximeter.
evidence: The claim describes the acquisition method.

claim: Gradients were applied along 30 isotropic directions with b = 1200 s/mm2.
source: Gradients were applied along 30 isotropic directions (Jones et al., 1999) with b = 1200 s/mm2.
evidence: The claim describes the diffusion gradient parameters.

claim: Three non-diffusion-weighted images were acquired with b = 0 s/mm2.
source: Three non-diffusion-weighted images were acquired with b = 0 s/mm2.
evidence: The claim describes the acquisition of baseline diffusion images.

claim: ExploreDTI was used to correct for subject motion and eddy current distortions.
source: ExploreDTI (Leemans and Jones, 2009) was used to correct for subject motion and eddy current distortions.
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing method for diffusion data.

claim: The two-compartment 'free water elimination' procedure was implemented to correct for partial volume artefacts arising from voxel-wise free water contamination.
source: In order to correct for partial volume artefacts arising from voxel-wise free water contamination, the two-compartment 'free water elimination' procedure was implemented (Pasternak et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim describes a preprocessing method for diffusion data.

claim: Deterministic whole-brain WM tractography was performed using ExploreDTI based on constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD).
source: Deterministic whole-brain WM tractography was performed using ExploreDTI. Tractography was based on constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD; see Tournier et al., 2004; Jeurissen et al., 2011), which extracts peaks in the fibre orientation density function (fODF) at each voxel.
evidence: The claim describes the tractography method.

claim: The 'diffusion tensor' model is not sufficient when modelling the distribution of water displacement in more complex fibre configurations, such as crossing or kissing fibres.
source: The 'diffusion tensor' model is not sufficient when modelling the distribution of water displacement in more complex fibre configurations, such as crossing or kissing fibres (e.g., as seen where the anterior pillars of the fornix meet the anterior commissure).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about limitations of the diffusion tensor model.

claim: The fODF quantifies the proportion of fibres in a voxel pointing in each direction and so information about more complex fibre configurations can be extracted.
source: The fODF—which is estimated directly by CSD—quantifies the proportion of fibres in a voxel pointing in each direction and so information about more complex fibre configurations can be extracted (Jones, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about fODF and is supported by a citation.

claim: Each streamline was reconstructed using an fODF amplitude threshold of 0.1 and a step size of 1 mm.
source: Each streamline was reconstructed using an fODF amplitude threshold of 0.1 and a step size of 1 mm and followed the peak in the fODF that resulted in the smallest step-wise change in orientation.
evidence: The claim describes the tractography parameters.

claim: An angle threshold of 30° was used and any streamlines exceeding this threshold were terminated.
source: An angle threshold of 30° was used and any streamlines exceeding this threshold were terminated.
evidence: The claim describes the tractography parameters.

claim: To generate three-dimensional reconstructions of each tract, 'way-point' ROIs were manually drawn onto whole-brain FA maps in the diffusion space of individual subjects.
source: To generate three-dimensional reconstructions of each tract, 'way-point' ROIs were manually drawn onto whole-brain FA maps in the diffusion space of individual subjects (Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim describes the tractography ROI method.

claim: A multiple ROI approach was used to reconstruct the fornix.
source: A multiple ROI approach was used to reconstruct the fornix (Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim describes the tractography method for the fornix.

claim: Fibre-tracking of the ILF was performed using a two-ROI approach in each hemisphere.
source: Fibre-tracking of the ILF was performed using a two-ROI approach in each hemisphere (Wakana et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim describes the tractography method for the ILF.

claim: Voxel-wise statistical analysis of the DTI data was carried out using TBSS.
source: Voxel-wise statistical analysis of the DTI data was carried out using TBSS (for a full description, see Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim describes the analysis method for DTI data.

claim: TBSS permits voxel-wise correlations by non-linearly projecting all subjects' DTI data (MD or FA) onto a mean tract skeleton before applying voxel-wise cross-subject statistics.
source: TBSS permits voxel-wise correlations by non-linearly projecting all subjects' DTI data (MD or FA) onto a mean tract skeleton before applying voxel-wise cross-subject statistics.
evidence: The claim describes how TBSS works.

claim: Clusters were extracted using Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement with a FWE-corrected threshold of p = 0.05.
source: To address the possibility of reporting false-positives, clusters were extracted using Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement (Smith and Nichols, 2009) with a FWE-corrected threshold of p = 0.05.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical thresholding method.

claim: Functional MRI data were preprocessed using FEAT (FSL).
source: Functional MRI data were preprocessed using FEAT (FSL, www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl) and involved: motion correction (Jenkinson et al., 2002), removal of non-brain tissue using BET (Smith, 2002), spatial smoothing using a 5 mm full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel, mean-based intensity normalisation, and high-pass temporal filtering (Gaussian-weighted least squares straight line fitting, with sigma = 50.0 s).
evidence: The claim describes the fMRI preprocessing steps.

claim: Time-series statistical analysis was carried out using FMRIB's Improved Linear Model (FILM) with local autocorrelation correction.
source: Time-series statistical analysis was carried out using FMRIB's Improved Linear Model (FILM) with local autocorrelation correction (Woolrich et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim describes the fMRI analysis method.

claim: Registration to high-resolution 3D anatomical T1 scans and to a standard MNI 152 template image was carried out using FLIRT.
source: Registration to high-resolution 3D anatomical T1 scans (per participant) and to a standard MNI 152 template image (for group averaging) was carried out using FLIRT (Jenkinson and Smith, 2001; Jenkinson et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim describes the registration method for fMRI data.

claim: A bilateral ROI of the HC was extracted from the Harvard–Oxford subcortical atlas using FSL and was defined using a probability threshold of 50%.
source: A bilateral ROI of the HC was extracted from the Harvard–Oxford subcortical atlas (Jovicich et al., 2009) using FSL and was defined using a probability threshold of 50%.
evidence: The claim describes the ROI definition method.

claim: The PrC was based on a probabilistic mask from the literature and defined using a probability threshold of 50%.
source: The PrC was based on a probabilistic mask from the literature (Devlin and Price, 2007) and likewise defined using a probability threshold of 50%.
evidence: The claim describes the ROI definition method.

claim: The FFA was approximated by intersecting an anatomical mask of the fusiform gyrus with a probabilistic map of face activations thresholded at 50%.
source: The FFA was approximated by intersecting an anatomical mask of the fusiform gyrus (from the Harvard–Oxford cortical atlas) with a probabilistic map of face activations thresholded at 50% (Atlas of Social Agent Perception, http://www.andrewengell.com/wp; see Engell and McCarthy, 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the ROI definition method.
